title: Volatile Evidence
summary: Volatile evidence is data that exists only while a system is running or powered, such as the contents of memory, running processes, open network connections, logged in sessions, mounted file systems, temporary files, and encryption keys held in random access memory. It is destroyed by shutdown, restart, or even by a process exiting normally, which is why incident response practice orders collection from the most volatile sources to the least volatile. In real environments it appears in live response triage, memory capture for malware analysis, and recovery of keys needed to read a fully encrypted disk. The mistake investigators make is following the older instinct to pull the power plug first: that destroys memory resident artefacts, and on a modern system it may also leave an encrypted host unreadable forever. Where that choice must be made, the trade off is usually documented and weighed against the risk of letting the intruder keep operating.

beginner.definition: Volatile evidence is information that disappears when a computer is switched off. Examples include running programs, open network connections and the contents of memory. It is different from evidence on a disk, which stays after a shutdown. Investigators must collect volatile evidence first, while the machine is still running.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some of the most useful clues about an attack exist only in memory. They show which programs were running and where data was being sent. Switching the computer off destroys all of it in a single moment. On an encrypted computer, switching off may also lock the disk away forever. Knowing what to capture first often decides whether an investigation succeeds.
howItWorks: Responders decide whether the machine must stay on, weighing risk against evidence loss.
They capture the contents of memory first, because that changes and disappears fastest of all.
They record the running processes, open network connections and the users who are logged in.
They note temporary files, mounted drives and scheduled jobs while the system lives.
They keep a written record of every command and every step, with times.
Only after volatile items are safe do they move to disk images and longer storage.
beginner.example: Think of a patient who suddenly becomes unwell at night in a hospital. A good nurse takes the temperature, the blood pressure and a blood sample immediately, because those signs change within minutes. The paper file on the shelf can wait until morning, since it will still be there. A computer works the same way: memory is the living patient, and the disk is the file on the shelf.
takeaways: Collect the fastest changing evidence first, because shutdown destroys it permanently.
Do not switch off or reboot a suspect machine without a documented decision.
Record every command and its time, so another investigator can trust your work.

objectives: Explain what volatile evidence is and give examples of it.
Describe the order of volatility and why it guides collection.
Explain why memory capture can decide the outcome of an investigation.
Describe the risk of shutting down a fully encrypted system.
Explain how documentation supports the reliability of collected evidence.
Describe how a responder records the decision to keep a system powered on.
